title: The Map shows 25 Skills, so no Tile's area lies

statements.says: Every Tile gets at least a fiftieth of the Map.
The Map shows at most 25 Skills.
The Filter and the order key choose which 25 Skills the Map shows.
The floor becomes a flat fiftieth at every size, and the guard that shrank it is no longer needed.
A Skill is off the Map for one of two different reasons: it had no figure to be sized by, or it had a figure and did not fit.
Each reason a Skill is off the Map gets its own line beneath the Map, naming the Skills.
A reader who wants the tail flips the order key.
The floor keeps a barely used Skill large enough to read and to click.
25 is the largest count for which the floor and its own guard both hold exactly.
The floor cannot hold at any size: fifty-one Skills at a fiftieth each is more than the whole Map.

The code shrank the floor as the count grew, to min(2%, 0.5/n), so the promise quietly weakened past 25 Skills and was half of itself at 50, and nothing on screen and no test said where it stopped holding.
A floor is a lie about area: with four Skills at 1000, 1, 1 and 0.5, the last is a two thousandth of the total and was drawn at a fiftieth, forty times too big.
Two floored Tiles look the same size when one may be a hundred times the other, and comparing areas is the whole job of the Map.
A cap makes the rule true instead of writing down where it stops.
Nobody looks at the middle of the order.
Fifty Tiles with the guard dropped was rejected, because fifty at a fiftieth each fills the whole Map, so in a long tail every Tile sits on the floor at the same size and no picture is left.
Marking a floored Tile on screen was rejected, because in a real catalogue the long tail is mostly floored, so the mark would cover most of the Map and make the glance harder rather than truer.
Writing the limit down and leaving the Map alone was rejected, because it keeps a Map whose areas cannot be trusted and asks the reader to remember when.
